cells.king: The beginning of the record is lost and consequently the name of the king and his regnal year are not available; but the details of the date, Śu', trītiya, Wednesday and Uttara are found
cells.reference: SITI, Vol. iii, part, i. No. 1189, Page no. 1184.
cells.remarks: The record registers an order of the king issued while he was seated in the garden Vañji nāyakan tirunandavanam witnessing the dance after worshipping the God, granting the village Minnuvānpalli alias Alagiya-Chōlā-Kūttanūr in Tatṭtaiyūrnādu, fixing its revenue at 30 poṇ, to meet the expenses of worship, offerings, various other expenditures and the special festival in the month of Māśi to god Alagiya-Chokkanātha, who was installed in the temple of Tiruvānilaiudaiya Mahādēva at Karuvūr, which was Vañji-mānagaram alias Mudivalaṅgu-Chōlapuram in Veṅgālanādu, a division of Vīraśōlā-maṇdalam. The name Alagiri is found mentioned in the inscription. From the tenor of the record it is possible to take him as the donor. We know that Alagiri Nāyaka, the foster-brother of the Madurai Nāyaka ruler Chokkanātha Nāyaka, was in charge of this country for some time and that his inscriptions are found in the area. But the means of the signatories to the record point to an earlier period. Probably the king was a member of the Pāṇdya line of Madurai of the 13th or early 14th century A.D.

cells.remarks: The record is complementary to the above one. Karkadai Trailōkyan alias Kōdanđarāman of Kođumāllūr left the land purchased by him from the sabhā of Ariñjikai-chaturvēdimangalam with the sabhā themselves to be cultivated by them and to use the produce of the land for the maintenance of a boat in their tank in the following way; 60 kālam of paddy annually as wages to each of the 6 labourers engaged for the boat; 45 kālam annually to the supervisor (kanċāṇi) to each of the carpenters and the blacksmiths who repaired the boat two kālam, 1 tūṇi and 1 padakku; to the valaiyar who supplied wood 2 kālam. It was stipulated that the band of workers should dredge the tank and bring the silt-mud on the boat four times a day at the rate of 140 baskets each time to be applied to the banks. The basket's capacity was put at tūṇi and a padakku. The sabhā agreed to discharge the duty assigned to them.

cells.reference: ARE, 1922, no. 357; Ibid., part ii, p. 111.
cells.remarks: Records gift of land in Marudūr in Urattūr-kūrram to two individuals named Nārāyaṇa-bhatta alias Madhurāntaka-Brahmarāya and Tiruvarangamāli-bhatta alias Kulasēkhara-Brahmarāya belonging to Vikramachōla-chaturvēdimangalam in Ēriyūr-nāđu, a s.d. of Pāṇdikulapati-valaṇāđu for providing offerings to the deity of Tirumalīśvara-muđaiya-Nāyanār at Vēmbaṇūr for the prosperity of the country. It is said that the revenue expected for the 6th and 7th year from the village of Marudūr failed ás there were no people to cultivate the fields. To make good the loss to the State, the whole nāđu undertook to bear the burden, and in this document, the villages, the cities and the nāđu of Kađaladaiyāđaolangaikonda-chōla valaṇāđu agreed among themselves to give away Marudūr to the two individuals mentioned above. Pillai Mābali Vāṇarāyar was incharge of Kōnāđu alias Kadaladaiyad-Ilangevkonđachōla-valaṇāđu.

cells.findspot: Found while digging for the foundation of a house at Anbil, Lālguđi taluk of the Tiruchi rāppalji District. The plates are 11 in number, the ring carries a well-executed seal, which bears, in half relief, the figures of a tiger, two carp fishes, bow, two lamp-stands, two chauris and an umbrella and the legend in Śanskrit verse round the margin of the seal declaring that it is the irrevocable edict of Rājakēsarivarman
cells.remarks: After invoking the blessings of Lakshmi, Hari and Śiva, the mythical genealogy of the Chōla family is given; Vishnu, Brahma, Marīchi, Kāśyapa, Aryaman, Mahāvira, Rudrajit, Chandrajit, Uśinara, Sibi. In this family after many kings like Śenni, Killi and Karikāla passed away, was born Kōchchengannāṇ, who built temples for Śiva in all countries; his son was Nallatīkkōṇ. Then came Vaļabha, then, Śrīkantha. Then came Vijayālaya, the above of Victory; his son Rājakēsari built many temples of stone on both the banks of the river Kāvēri from the Sahya mountain to the ocean; his son Vīra-chōla reduced Madura to a wretched condition, married the daughter of a Kērala king called Paluvēttaraiyar; his son was Arīnchika who markried Kalyāni, daughter of a Vaidumba king; their son was Sundara-chōla. Aniruddh a, the chief minister of Sundara-Chōla, is praised for his wisdom and noble qualities. He had his residence at the agrahāra village called Prēma. His father was Nārāyaṇa; his mother made an endowment for providing sumptuous meals to a learned Brahmana daily at Śrīraṅgam. This minister, who belonged to the Āvēnika-gōtra and the Jamini sūtra, was granted by the king the village called Karuṇākaramaṅgalam measuring 10 vēlis of land, in Nalvilānkuđi in the Alundūrmahārāstra, inclusive of all the taxes, kārāṇmai, mīyātchi and antara. He was also conferred upon the title Brahmādhirāja. Aravaṇaiyāṇ, alias Pallava Muddhādhirāja, was the executor of the grant. The Tamil portion is addressed to the brahmadēyak-kiļavar, the nādu and the dēvadāna, pallichchaṇda and kāṇimuṛmūttu villages of Tiruvalundūr-nādu informing them that ten vēli of land situated in Naṇmulānkuđi in their Nādu were given away as ekabhogam to Nārāyāṇa Aniruddhan alias Pallava-Muttaraiyan was designated as the executor of the grant. They who received the royal order fixed accordingly the boundaries of the granted village. The grantee was given the privilege of enjoying the rights of Kārāṇmai and mivāṭchi and the revenue from all taxes including maṇṇupādu, ilaikkūlam, tarip-puḍavai, kaṇṇālakkāṇam and aṅgāđip-pāttam. The Sanskrit prasasti is said to have been composed by Mādhava Bhatta vajvan who was the son of Bhatta Datta of the Parāśraya vamsa, and who wąs a very learned man and a disciple of Srīnātha. The document was written down by the madhyastha of Pāmburam, called Brahma-maṅgalliyan and it was engraved by the smith Virachōla.

cells.remarks: Records a gift of 60 kāśu by the Pallava king Nandhipōttaraiyar 'who conquered in the battle of Tellāru', for maintaining a perpetual lamp in the temple of Tirutavatturai Mahādēvar in Idaiyārru-nāđu. The amount was entrusted to the sabhā of Nallimaṅgalam in the same nāđu, who undertook to provide ghee for the lamp. The sabhā also bound themselves to the mūlappaṭta-paṅ-māhēśvarar of the temple, owing that if they failed in their duty, they should pay a fine of 216 kāṇam. NOTE:- The proximity of this record to the one (SII, xiv, 12) on the same wall belonging to the Pāndya king Mārāṇjadaiyaṇ alias Varaguna-mahārāja, and the mode of dating in a similar manner make this record assignable to the same Pāndya king. See also EI, xxviii, p. 39.

cells.remarks: Records sale of land called Tolunervēli measuring a vēli to the temple of Mahādēvar at Tiruttavatturai in Idaiyārru-nadu for 50 kaļāņju of gold, for providing sacred food offerings and burning a perpetual lamp in the temple. The gold included 30 kaļāņju donated to the temple for a lamp by Pūdikanḍan of Kavirapporkatti in Idaiyārru-nādu and 20 kaļāņju belonging to the temple itself. The four vendors including the duvēdi (Dviyēdin) Nakkanūran, Chāvānti-Nārāyana-Mahādēvan, Nārāyanan Chēndan and Nārāyanan Nakkan sold the said land in Chirukavūr, in the mīkūru of Kalārk-kūrram, a s.d. of Maļa-nādu on the northern bank (of the Kāvēri), with all the adjuncts, i.e. illavalākam (house site), tōttam (house garden) akaiyāru, puñjey and nañjey. The land had been gifted as iraiyili to the religious preceptor (gurukkal) of the vendors. The land was exempted from the tax burden including irai, echchōru, vetti, vedinai, chennīr-vetti and other vettis. The sale was endorsed by the sabhā of Teṅgangudi.

cells.remarks: Registers a gift of 30 kalañju of gold by Nangai Varagunaperumānār, the sister of Chōlaperumānadigal (i.e. Sundarachōla). For this amount the sabhā of Manalkāl sold half a vēli of land to the temple of īŚvara-Bhatṭāraka at Tiruttavatturai in Idaiyārru-nādu for maintaining a lamp in the temple. The sabhā of Manalkāl which was a brahmadēya in the mēlkūru of Kalārk-Kūrram in Mala-nādu on the north bank (of the Kāvēri) remitted all the taxes from the land including chennīr-veṭti and other veṭtis, irai, echchōru and vēdinai. The sabhā undertook to protect the land from any future impediments, failing which they were liable to a fine at the hands of the māhēśvaras themselves in favour of the king including the nilaikkalam either severally or individually.

cells.remarks: Records a sale of land, 6 mā and odd in extent, free of taxes by the mahāsabhā of Nityavīnitamaṅgalam a brahmadēya in Idaiyārru-nāđu to the temple of Isvara-Bhaṭara at Tiruttavatturai, for 30 kalanju of gold which had been endowed to the temple for burning a perpetual lamp by Śaṅkaraṇ Kunrappōlan of Puttūr in Malai nāđu on behalf of Kōkilānadigalār, the daughter of Sēramānār (Chēra king). This evidently refers to the queen of Parantaka I of that name, though she is not specifically referred to as such in the record. Nityavīnitamaṅgalam which finds mention already is a record of Ādiyta I (SII, XIII, no. 325) should have been so named after the surname 'Nityavīnita' for a Pallava ruler, possibly Nandivarman III, an inscription of whom is found in the temple (Tp....., ARE, 1929, no. 120).

cells.remarks: Begins with a Sanskrit verse stating that this is a record in the Paśchimadvāra issued by the Māhēśvaras. Records a samayaśāsaṇa bestowed by a congregation of the Śrī-Rudra-māhēśvaras and the māhēśvaras of many Mandalas and some other bodies at the Nārpattennāyiravantirukkāyaṇam in the temple of Tāyilunallīśyaram uđaiyār in Mēlaittiruvāsal in Śrīmāhēśvaranallūr in Mīmalai-nādu at the instance of the deity Chandēśvara, granting some land as silpācharya-kāni and also some honours and privileges of the samaya on Tillainayakaṇ alias Tiruttavatturai-āchāriyan and his brother for their services to the said temple and to the samaya. Tillaināyakaṇ is said to have been the Tacchāchāriyaṇ of Maṇakkāl alias Virudarajabhayankara-chaturvēdi-maṅgalam in the Kīlmuṛi of Mala-nādu.

cells.remarks: The king is said at the beginning to have wrested the country after his victory at Tellāru. Records a raid by Māvali-yaniyasthāna-mālyān Sēvaṇan causing the destruction of a maṭha and the death of the chief priest ('guravar) and his disciple, a brāhmaṇa called Chattimurrattēvār, who offered resistance to save the matha. The temple of Arīṇdikai-Iśvaragriham at Parāntakapuram is mentioned. Note: The names of the temple and the village might have been made after the Chōla Arīṇjiya and his father Parāntaka I. In that case the record must be a later copy of the original record.

cells.remarks: Records the gift of 60 paṇam annually to meet the expenditure on various services during the celebration of the Vaikāśi festival of god Tirumaṇalmēđuđaiyār by the Vāṇiyanagarattār belonging to the Padinenbhumi. The prasasti of the vāṇiya-nagārattār lists Kikkindai (Kishkinda)—their mountain, Pampai (Pampā)—their river, Garuđa—their flag, Saimukkiya—their insignia, Jayavāranam—their elephant, Kalimārutam—their horse, Kamala—kanđikai—their chariot and Tōṇrimalai—their garland. It further claims that they guilded the temple of Kambar and gave Lakshmi (tirumagal) in marriage to Marudar whose identity is not clear.

cells.remarks: Records sale of land made tax-free by the Mūlaparuđai of Tiruvellarai a tāṇiyūr in Vađavali-nāđu, a s.d. of Rājaśraya-valanāđu of Uđaiyān Vankadaṇ Saṅkaraṇ alias Daṇdanāyakaṇ Rājādhirāja-Pallavaraiyan of Uttama-chōlar-nallūr, a perundanam officer of the king. The land was situated in Kalvaṇ maṅgalam in Kalārk-kūrram, a s.d. of Rājaśraya-valanāđu. The purchaser made over the land to the matha called Chēndamaraikkannan-matha attached to the Periya-Šrī-Kōyil temple at Tiruvellarai as Sālābhōga for feeding brāhmanas and Yōgins. It is said Kalvaṇmaṅgalam had been granted to the Mūlaparuḍai as abhishēka-dakshiṇa free of taxes.

cells.date: r.y. 27, 'who took all countries.' Kumbha. ba. 11, Friday, Uttirādam = Friday, 11 February, A.D. 1295
cells.reference: ARE, 1938-39, no. 189, Ibid., part II, para. 30.
cells.remarks: Commences with a panegyric of the agricultural community called Chitramēli-periyanāttār, the members of which call themselves 'Bhūmiputras' and the 'children of Ayyāpolil-Paramēśvari', whom 'the plough-share was the deity and the pedlar's pack (paśumpai) their torch'. They bear a number of other birudas indicative of their prosperity. States that as Mudaliyār Tavapperumāl Muḍaliyār under-took to complete the unfinished Periyanāttān-tirumāligai and Periyanēttān-Tiru-gōpuram in the temple of Tiruppaiñ-ñili-udaiya-Nāyanār, the nāḍu nagaram, agaram, and brahmadēya-tenants of the Periyanāttār community agreed to contribute for this purpose, a specified quantity of paddy and money per vēli of land.

States that as Mudaliyār Tavapperumāl Muḍaliyār under-took to complete the unfinished Periyanāttān-tirumāligai and Periyanēttān-Tiru-gōpuram in the temple of Tiruppaiñ-ñili-udaiya-Nāyanār, the nāḍu nagaram, agaram, and brahmadēya-tenants of the Periyanāttār community agreed to contribute for this purpose, a specified quantity of paddy and money per vēli of land.

cells.match_text: SII Vol. XII Pt I, No. 40
cells.remarks: Dantivarman is said to have been born in the Pallavatilaka family which sprang from the Bhāradāvja-gōtra. Records that one Kamban Araiyan, the brother of Visaiyanallūlān of Ālambākkam began the digging of a great well at Teṇnūr, a suburb of Tiruvellarai, in the 4th year of the king and finished it in the 5th year and named it as Mārpidugu-peruṅgiṇaṇu. A verse following this record, apparently forming part of this, pointing to the transient nature of the worldly life, enjoins all to do some charitable deed even before they are caught in the clutches of the old age, so as to perpetuate their name.

cells.remarks: At first the king Danti-Nandivarman, the Pallava-Mahārājadhirāja Paramēśvaran, is said to have belonged to the Bhāradvāja gōtra and the Brahmakshatrakula. cells.remarks: Registers a decision of Mūla-parishat of Tiruvellarai of Vāśudēva-vinṇagar Emberumāṇ of Naraśingamangalam, a hamlet of Tiruvellarai with regard to the lease of some village belonging to Perumāl Ulaguđaiya Nāyanār (Rājarāja III). According to the decision, the existing committee of four members was replaced by another consisting of eight who should settle the kađamai and Kuđimai dues to be collected on lands therein. The members of the committee were remunerated for their service and were to be changed annually. It was further ruled that a person who once served on this committee should not be selected again for the next four years.

cells.remarks: Records on the orders of the araiyar Āchārakānta-Brahmādhirāja, the mūlaparađai of Mahēndramaṅgalm, a brahmadēya, constituted a new vāriyam (committee) consisting of a kaṇakku and certain members (vāriyar) to take stock of the tax-free dēvadāna lands belonging to the temple of Tirukkutakkutturāi-Perumānadigal in the village and to make provisions for the various services in the temple. The details of allocations of fields for each service are elaborately given. It is said that provision was made for seven persons to play music during the śrībali service three for mattali, one for Karađigai, one for talam, one for pāđagam and one for śēgan-digi.

cells.remarks: Registers a compact drawn up by the Srutimans of Ūrrattūr, assembled in the maṇdapa of the temple called Uttama-chōlaṇ, for the community of Idangai classes. Narrates in detail the origin of the Idangai classes of 98 sub-sects, as described by themselves. "While, in order to kill the demons (that disturbed) the sacrifices of the sage Kāśyapa, they were made to appear from the agni-kuṇda and while they were protecting he said sacrifice, Charkravartin Arindama honoured the officiating sage-priests carrying them in a car and led them to a Brāhmana colony (newly founded by himself). On this occasion they were made to take their seats on the back side of the car and to carry the slippers and umbrellas of the sages. Eventually with these Brahmana sages they also were made to settle down in the villages of Tiruvellarai, Pāchchil, Tiruvāśi, Tiruppidavūr, Ūrrattūr and Kāraikkādu of Chennivalakūrram (all of which are now situated in the Tiru-chirāppalli District). They received the clan name Idangai because the sages (while they got down from their cars) were supported by them on their left side. The ancestors of this sect having lost their credentials and insignia in jungles and bushes they were ignorant of their origin. Having now once learnt it, they, the members of the 98 sub-sects entered into a compact, in the 40th year of the king, that they should thereafter behave like the sons of the same parents and what good or evil might befall on any of them, would be shared by all. If anything derogatory happened to the Idangai class, they would jointly assert their rights till they established them. It was also understood that only those who, during their congregational meetings settle communal disputes, displayed the birudas of horn, bugle a parasel should belong to their class. Those who had to recognise them then and thereafter, in public, must do so from their distinguishing symbols—the feather of the crane and the loose-having hair (?). The horn and conch-shell should also be sounded in front of them and the bugle blown according to the fashion obtained among the Idangai people. Those who acted in contravention to these rules should be treated as the enemies of their class. Those who behaved differently from the rules prescribed for the conduct of Idangai classes should be excommunicated and should not be recognized as srutimans. They would be considered slaves of the classes who were opposed to them." It is said that this document was got engraved in the temple at Ūrrattūr and in that at Tiruppaññili.

cells.remarks: Records gift of 6 kaļańju of gold by Arińjikai Pānđan of Allūr to the pattuđaiyār of the temple from the interest of which they agreed to fetch water from the river Kāviri for the sacred bath of the deity for the services daily. It is stated that kalam was to be blown during the conveyance of the water. cells.remarks: Records gift of 90 kalāṇju of śemmai gold from the interest of which the sabhā of Tiruvaraṅgam undertook to feed 4 Brāhmanas daily in the temple of Sri Araṅgattu-Perumānadigal. The donor was one Puttadigal son of Kārāṇai Vilupperariayar Arivāladigal. The annaul interest was fixed at 1 kalam and 1 tīṇi of paddy per kalaṇju. The sabha of Tiruvaraṅgam (Śrīraṅgam) undertakes to supply 120 kalam of ripe (old) paddy annually measured out with the measure called śennaḍaikkāl for the interest on the endowed amount.

text.remarks: Seems to record a gift of land, purchased for the purpose, the god by Vaṇdālañchēri-udaiyān Vellālan Ānai..... alias Vāṇakōvaraiyan of Tirunaraiyūr included in Kulōttungachōła-valaṇādu having assembled the Penūnguri-sabhā of the brahmadēya village Arīndigai-chaturvēdi-maṅgalam in the temple of Tiruk-kuruṅgudi-Ālvān. The gift seems to have been intended for meeting the expenses of the sacred bath of the deity on the day of Ēkādaśi. Another fragment dated in the 32nd year of the king also mentions the same donor and seems to refer to a similar donation by him.

cells.reference: ARE, 1938-39, no. 113; Ibid., part II, para. 23; SII. XXIV, no. 142.
cells.match: <button type="button" class="xref-link" data-corpus="sii" data-key="sii|xxiv||142" data-url="SII-Inscriptions.html">SII Vol. XXIV, No. 142</button>
cells.remarks: Refers to the erosion of the river Kolliđam into the lands belonging to the temple at Śrīraṅgam and Tiruvānaikkā and the re-settlement of the proper boundaries by arbitration under orders of the king Annavāyiluđaiyān Gāngeyarāyar (Kulōttunga III), in his 20th year and 213th day through the officer Gāngēyarāyar and puravuvari-nāyakan cheyyār officers to settle the boundary, who, in consultation with the representatives of both the temples, representatives from the sabhā, accountants of the two villages and the superintendants of both the temples, adjudged their award by taking into account the holdings of the two temples as they were before the erosion in the 19th year of king Kulōttunga (c. 1197), and the actual enjoyment-rights of both the parties and by suggesting suitable exchange of lands in some cases. This award satisfied both the parties and they demarcated their respective portions by planting boundary-stones with the mark of tiruvālī (chakra) and sūla.

cells.remarks: Registers a gift of the village Munōmbūṭti alias Śrīranganallūr in Pattaiya-nāđu as tiruvidaiyāṭtam to the god. The Sanskrit verse delineates the chicfs genealogy as: Kalikāla of the Śōlār race, in the family Dāya-Bhīma, his son Petta, his son Erāsiddhi and his son from Śrīdēvi, Tammusiddhi who was the younger brother (anujanma) of Manmasiddhi. The gift village and the district in which it lay are mentioned respectively as Mṇōmaṇi and Paintarāshtra in the Sanskrit verse. The record ends with a sentence stating that similār record may be engraved in the temple at Tirupparkadāl in Nellūr.

cells.remarks: Records a gift of 1,00,000 kāśu to the temple by Deviyar* Sōmaladēviyār for a lamp and a flower garden 50,000 kāśu out of the endowment is said to have been contributed from the treasury (bhaṇḍāram) of the queen Sōmaladēviyār and the balance by Padinenvishaya Brahma-Chakravartigał of Vaṅgippuram and Taṇnantulāydāśār, a dasa-nambi, in equal shares of 25,000 kāśu. The former amount was set apart for the supply of ghee for the lamps (kāṭpūra-maṇivilakku) and out of the latter, two plots of land 8 ma in extent for a flower garden for 20,000 kāśu and 3 vēli for 30,000 kāśu for maintaining four gardeners for the upkeep of the garden were purchased.

cells.match: <button type="button" class="xref-link" data-corpus="sii" data-key="sii|xxiv||193" data-url="SII-Inscriptions.html">SII Vol. XXIV, No. 193</button>
cells.remarks: Registers the ulvari issued by the king at the instance of Aiyyaṇ Malavarāyan for the tax-free village Kumaranambinallūr newly formed and granted to the temple by Nāvāyan Koṇdanambi of Kuļamūkku, a horse-dealer of Malaimanđalam, for worship and offerings. Refers to Iratṭakāla-puram, for which a portion of the land was separated to form the new village. Aiyyaṇ Malavarāyan at whose instance the lands in question were exempted from tax and Araiyan Viratamudittān alias Pallavarāyan of Chakrapāṇinallūr in Sewvirukkai-nāđu are well known to be high officers who served under Māravarman Sundara Pāṇdya II (A.D. 1232-49) (SII. V, no. 448) and therefore this inscription which is dated in the third year opposite to the eleventh (A.D. 1245-46) may be assigned to him.

cells.match: <button type="button" class="xref-link" data-corpus="sii" data-key="sii|xxiv||203" data-url="SII-Inscriptions.html">SII Vol. XXIV, No. 203</button>
cells.remarks: Begins with the introduction Samstajagadādhāra, etc. Records an order issued at the request of the king by the god himself while seated with his consorts on the 'Būpālarāyan' lion-throne in the bedchamber of the temple. It states that the administration of the temple was hitherto conducted by a body of ten persons belonging to the Kōvaṇavar-kottu. The benefactions of the king are then recounted. Sundara Pāṇdya (I) is said to have defined the activities on the temple, made gifts as aḍukkaļaippuram for the maintenance of the kitchen, instituted services, gilded the Vimānas like Šrīranga Vimāna as also Sundara-Pāṇdyan-madil and the gōpura, made duplicate sets of ornaments for the god, constructed palanquin (sivigai) and presented several other articles made of gold. This increase in the wealth of the temple necessitated closer supervision and consequently a change in the management, which was now entrusted to a body of ten, not exclusively of Kōvaṇavar as hitherto, but selected 2 from the Kōvaṇavar, 2 from Šrīrangamaraiyōr, 1 from Tōduvattuttūmaraiyōr, 2 from Taļai-iđuvar, 1 from Vāšál Āriyyar and 2 from Arattjimukki-Anukkar. The inscription is attested by the Royal Secretary Kanṇuđaiyān Pallavan Vilupparaiyan of Puduchchēri, and it is said to have been engraved at the instance of Šrīranganārāyana-Dāśan, Māttūr-Kilavan Kurukulattaraiyan, the manager of the temple (Vittukkariyamaraygira), the Kōvaṇavar and the Kuđavar.

This increase in the wealth of the temple necessitated closer supervision and consequently a change in the management, which was now entrusted to a body of ten, not exclusively of Kōvaṇavar as hitherto, but selected 2 from the Kōvaṇavar, 2 from Šrīrangamaraiyōr, 1 from Tōduvattuttūmaraiyōr, 2 from Taļai-iđuvar, 1 from Vāšál Āriyyar and 2 from Arattjimukki-Anukkar. The inscription is attested by the Royal Secretary Kanṇuđaiyān Pallavan Vilupparaiyan of Puduchchēri, and it is said to have been engraved at the instance of Šrīranganārāyana-Dāśan, Māttūr-Kilavan Kurukulattaraiyan, the manager of the temple (Vittukkariyamaraygira), the Kōvaṇavar and the Kuđavar.

cells.remarks: Records Sundara Pāṇdya's building operations at, and gift to, the Raṅganātha temple. He built a shrine for Narasimha and another for Vishṇu's attendant Viṣvaksēna both of which were covered with gold, and a gilt tower which contained an image of Narasimha. He covered the central shrine of the temple with gold, on account of which achievement he assumed, the surname Hēmachchandarāja. He placed in the shrine golden image of Vishṇu. He also covered the inner wall of the central shrine with gold and built in front of it, a dining hall, which he provided with golden vessels. In the course of two 'dining weeks', he provided for food offerings to the god. In the month of Chaitra he celebrated the 'procession-festival' of the god. He built a golden ship to celebrate Viharōtsva (sporting festival). The king built three golden domes (vimāna) respectively over the images of Hēmachchandanarāja-Hari and Garuḍa and the hall which contain the conch of Vishnu. He is said to have given large quantities of gold by repeatedly performing the ascending of the scales (tuladhiroha). The other gifts of the king mentioned in the record are the following: A garland of emerald taken (in war) from the treasure of the Kathaka king, a crown of jewels, a golden image of shēsha, a golden arch (makara-tōraṇa a pearl garland, a canopy (vithana) of pearls, a golden car (satanga), a golden trough (prapa), a golden image of Garuḍa; different kinds of fruits, undergarment, aureola, pedestal armour, vessels and throne, all in gold. The king is said to have seized Śrīranga from a king who is designated as "the Moon of Karnāta", and plundered the capital of the Kathaka king.

cells.match: <button type="button" class="xref-link" data-corpus="sii" data-key="sii|viii||633" data-url="SII-Inscriptions.html">SII Vol. VIII, No. 633</button>
cells.remarks: Recrods that a kudi-velĵāla called Karunādaka-Pulalavasettai who was born at Mahā-grāmam Kiraikottul and who was known to the king Ģaṅga-Perumānađi travelled through many countries trading in rubies and finally settled at Tanjayur in Chōlanāđu. He once visited Isāna-maṅgalam situated in Uraiyūr-kūrram on the south bank of the Kāvēri supposed to be the Dakshiṇa-Gaṅgai and desired to perform a charitable deed there. As requested by the sabhā of the village he erected on the western portion of the village a Vishnu shrine called Pulalaya-Viṇṇagar after himself and consecrated there an image brought from the north. The shrine was placed under the protection of the "four hundred" of the Parudai of the village and the Vaishṇavas.

cells.findspot: On two pillars in a rock-cut cave near the summit of the hill at Tiruchchirāppalli
cells.language: Sanskrit in florid Pallava Grantha characters, 29 lines
cells.remarks: The inscription on the left pillar alludes to the river Kāvēri as 'the beloved of the Pallaya (king)'. It also refers to king Guṇabhara as a worshipper of the linga and who left hostile conduct to embrace Śaivism. A statute of Satyasamdha (apparently the king) was put up on the hill. The hill is described as the diadem of the Chōla province and the Śiva temple on it as its chief jewel. The record on the right pillar stated that the king Gunabhara built a temple on the hill to Girisa (śiva) and placed a stone figure in it. The other birudas of the king mentioned in the inscription are Purushōt-tam and Satrumalla.

cells.remarks: In bold Pallava-Grantha and Tamil characters of an ornate nature belonging to the early 7th century. Pallava; Mahēndraman I, r.y. --- = accn. c. A.D. 610. These are the birudas of the Pallava king Mahēndravarman I arranged alphabetically and so engraved on the front face of the pillars. About fifty birudas are found, the important of which are the following : Vañjavalava, nitvavinita, navambu, nilfulemnevamby, naruku, tolpuka, nainika-mutrika, sankimnajati, antvaraga, vavasaya, Anvanibhajana, chittirakaralppuli, satyasandha, katuntarambu, karampu, vamkily, Lalitankura, Kurramby, vambara, gunabhara, terra, sharyabuddhi, etc. The name 'Mahendravikrama' is found mentioned in the inscription on the extreme left outer pillar, which contains also the birudas mattavilasa, mavamavakku, marumerra, macicheththakari, etc.

cells.remarks: Begins with the meykkīrtti Tirumagalpōla etc. Registers the sale of land, by the ūr of Sirṇambal and the patipāda-mūlanpattu-daip-pañchachārya dēvakaṇmis of the temple of Tribhuvanapati at Sirṇambal-Tiruchchirāppalli, lying in Ālaṅguđi in Vilattūr-nādu, a dēvadāna of the above temple, to Kamban-maniyan alias Vikramasinga-Mūvēndavēlāṇ, the Kilayan of Churalur in Churalur-kūrṇam for 5 kalāṇju. The purchaser was permitted to reclaim the land, bought, which he intended to use for the charity of feeding brahmanas, śivayōgins, and tapaśvins on all the nine days of the Chittirai festival. The gold realised for the price of the land was deposited with the paṇdāram of the temple.

Any trasagressor of the resolution of the sabhā was liable to a fine at the hands of the temple servant and the paṇmāhēśvaras of the seventy-eight nāđus.

text.remarks: Registers an endowment of land made by Bāláśiriyan Batṭaṇ Śivankūttan of Ādanūr to the temple of Tiruppāṇrurai-Mahādēva at Uttamasīli-chaturvēdimaṅgalam, a brahmadēya on the southern bank with the object of providing for the maintenance of temple servants engaged in sweeping the temple premises and bringing flowers for the deity and for the midday offerings. The deposited lump sum of 50 Ēlakkāsu with the sabhā of the village who agreed to pay themselves all the taxes due on the land including irai, siddhāyam, antarāyam, ūrtanisu, echchōṇu, etc. Some vāriyars (committee members) of the sabhā made necessary entries in the registers, nilamudal-pattākam and Kayttadi, concerning the remission of taxes on the land on the orders of the peruṅguri-sabhā assembled at the circumambulatory part of the Tiruveñnavāl-uđaiyār temple at Tiruvāṇaikkāval. Any trasagressor of the resolution of the sabhā was liable to a fine at the hands of the temple servant and the paṇmāhēśvaras of the seventy-eight nāđus.

cells.remarks: Registers gift of land by purchase from the peruṅguri-sabhā of Śrīkaṇṭha-chaturvēdimaṅgalam for the maintenance of four persons who were singing the Tīruppađiyam hymns in the Tiruverumbiyalvār temple with ūđukkai and talām daily during the three services. The donor was Vēlān Vīranārayānan alias Chembiyan Vēdivelār of Chiruđavūr who constructed the Śrīvimāṇa of the temple. The donor gave some gold to the same sabhā towards īraikāval (remission of taxes) and got the land exempted from the payment of all tax dues. He added this land to some other land whose boundary had been a matter of dispute between the sabhā of Śrīkaṇṭha-chaturyēdimaṅgalam and the ūr of Erumbiyūr and which he had bought and endowed to the temple for the same purpose. Note: The earlier donation is mentioned in the above record (SII. XIII, no. 50).

cells.remarks: Registers endowment of 2 veli and 7 ma of land by Vēlān Vīranārayānan alias Chembiyān Vēdivelār belonging to Chiruđavūr in Kiliyūrnāđu. The land was left in charge of the sabhā of Śrīkaṇṭha-chaturvēdimaṅgalam who received the īraikāvāl-dravyam from the donor towards the remission of taxes on the land. The object of the gift was to feed 15 brahmanas in the feeding house (chattiram) on the hill of Tiruverumbiyūr Ālyār every day. It was resolved that if anybody collected taxes on the land they should be fined some gold by the panmahēsvaras themselves. The document was written by the mađhyasthā of the village, Darmamapiriyān alias Kaliviśiyān Tarunendu-śēkharan.

cells.remarks: Refers to a decision (vyavastha) of the Penuiguqi-sabhā of Srīkaṅtha-chatūrvēdimaṅgalam assembled on the above date in the Tiruveṛumbiyūr-Ālvār temple that no taxes should be levied on the temple and its belongings by the sabhā. The assembly directed the sabhai-vāriyar in charge of the temple affairs for the year to inscribe the vyavasthā-patram on (the walls of) the śrīvimāna (central shrine) of the temple. The document was written down by the madhysthā of the village, Darmapriyan alias Kalivisaiyān Taranēndu-sēkharan.

cells.remarks: Registers the grant of a tax-free land measuring 29 vēli and odd in extent, in two villages under the name Ātiguṇakarpakanallūr, for the expenses of worship in the temple of Mahādēva at Uṛaiyūr in Uṛaiyūrkūrram, a s.d. of Kēralāntaka-valanāḍu. Reference is made to a temple of Villīsvara among the boundaries of the land granted. Subsidiary deities to whom separate offerings were made daily were Chandraśēkhara, Gaṇapati, Kōkaviṭanka and Urandai-Nāyaka.

cells.remarks: Records the deliberation of a complicated question of caste and the professions laid down to be followed by a certain anuloma class called Rathākaras who are described as the sons of Māhishyas by Karaṇi-women. On the strength of previous authorities such as Yājñavalkya, Gauthama, Kauṭilya, Bōdhāyana and others, the bhaṭṭas (the learned Brāhmaṇas) of Rājāśraya-chaturvēdi-maṅgalam defined (1) a Māhishya as one born of a kshatrīya father by a Vaisya mother, (2) a Karaṇi as the daughter of a Vaisya father by a sudra mother and (3) a Rathakara as the son of Māhishya father by karani mother. The following means of livelihood were also laid down for adoption by the Rathakaras: (1) Architecture; (2) Building coaches and chariots; (3) Erecting gōpuras of temples with images on them; (4) Preparation of instruments required by Brāhmaṇas in their sacrificial ceremonies such as late (srik), etc. (5) Building mandapas; (6) (not clear); (7) Making jewels for kings such as diadems, bracelets, etc. It was decided also that this anuloma sect of Rathakaras is superior to the pratiloma sect. One of the authorities quoted, also states that these Rathakaras were entitled to upanayana (the sacred-thread ceremony), iiya (performing sacrifices) and adhana (receiving the sacredfire). Another authority, however, suggests that the anulomas thus entitled to upanayana are forbidden from performing the agnihotra (keeping the sacredfire always alive) aupasana (worshipping the fire thus kindled), panchamahavijan (the five sacred duties prescribed for the Brāhmanas) viz., (i) devyajna (ceremonial worship of gods), (ii) pitriyajña (ceremonial worship of manes), (iii) brāhmayajña (ceremonial worship of rishis), (iv) bhutayajña (ceremonial worship of living creatures other than men) (v) manushayajña (ceremonial worship of men) and adhyayana (recital of the Vedas). The same authority also says that their upanayana ceremony ought not to be conducted by quoting the mantras (sacred hymns).

cells.match: <button type="button" class="xref-link" data-corpus="are" data-key="are|1906-10|c|1190" data-url="ARE-Inscriptions.html">ARE 1906-10, App. C, No. 29</button>
cells.remarks: After the date is the Sanskrit beginning with akuṅthōtkanṭha, which is a verbatim copy of a portion of the introduction in the copper-plates of the Gāhadēvāla king Gōvindachandra of Kanauj. Note: "It is unfortunate that the inscription was not finalised. The date of the Tamil portion, vīz., A.D. 1110-11 leaves us in doubt as to whether the Sanskrit passage, if complete, could belong to Madanapāla or his son Gōvindachandra. The latest known date of the former is A D. 1109 and the earliest date of the laiter is 1114. There is, however, no doubt that some sort of relationship existed between the Chōla king Kulōttunga I and the Gāhadāvālas of Kanauj. Perhaps either Madanapāla or his son Gōvindachandra or some other member of their family went to the Chōla capital Gangaikonđachōlapuram on a friendly visit to the Chola king Kulōttunga I and wished to make a grant to the temple. Accordingly, the genealogy of the donor was put in. For some reason or other either the grant itself was not made, or it was not engraved in full on stone."

cells.remarks: This registers an agreement by the Śivabrāhmanas headed by Kāsyapan Kunṇan Singa Bhattan and Bhāradvāji Korṇan Tiruvaranga-Bhattan of Periya Śrī Vānavanmahadevi-chaturvēdimangalam to Araiyan Śankaranavayanan alias Sōla Muttaraiyar that they would regularly conduct all the specified worship and offerings in the temple of Kailāsattu Ālvār constructed by him in the village for the endowment of land made by him under the Vađaguđi tank. The services comprised daily worship, special bath, offering and worship on the two Ayana-Sankrānti and two Vishu days and also on the day of Visākha in Vaigaśi month and the maintenance of a perpetual lamp. They bound themselves to be supervised by the Mahēśvara Nārpattennāyiravar and to pay fines in case of default to the Vāriya perumakka! of the assembly.

cells.remarks: Records that the sabhā of Pcriya-Vāṇavan Mahādēvi-chaturvēdimaṅgalam, a brahmadēya on the north bank received a sum of 200 kaļāņju of gold from a perundaram officer of Mummađi-chōļadēva (i.e. Rājarāja I) named Ambalavan-paļuvūrnakkan alias Vikrama-chōļa Mahārājan of Kuvalālam and gave the deed of agreement (ottōlai) waiving all the taxes on the land endowed by him to the temple of Paramasvāmin at Vijayamangalam. The temple was built by the officer himself. The taxes remitted included vāsalil pānda kuduriđu-varippadu, iřai, echchōņu, chenṇīr-vetti, etc. The sabhā resolved that if anybody among them levied the taxes aqting against the terms of their agreement he should be fined some gold by the dēvakaņmikaļ themselves. It is said the sabhā met in full strength at the Brahmasthāna in front of the Vinayābharaṇavinṇagar-Emberumān temple in the centre of village after announcing the same to the village by beating the drum (tattali-kotti) and blowing the trumpet (kālam-lādi)

text.reference: ARE, 1929, no. 168; SII. XIII, no. 76, pp. 36-37.
text.remarks: Records that the sabhā of Pcriya-Vāṇavan Mahādēvi-chaturvēdimaṅgalam, a brahmadēya on the north bank received a sum of 200 kaļāņju of gold from a perundaram officer of Mummađi-chōļadēva (i.e. Rājarāja I) named Ambalavan-paļuvūrnakkan alias Vikrama-chōļa Mahārājan of Kuvalālam and gave the deed of agreement (ottōlai) waiving all the taxes on the land endowed by him to the temple of Paramasvāmin at Vijayamangalam. The temple was built by the officer himself. The taxes remitted included vāsalil pānda kuduriđu-varippadu, iřai, echchōņu, chenṇīr-vetti, etc. The sabhā resolved that if anybody among them levied the taxes aqting against the terms of their agreement he should be fined some gold by the dēvakaņmikaļ themselves. It is said the sabhā met in full strength at the Brahmasthāna in front of the Vinayābharaṇavinṇagar-Emberumān temple in the centre of village after announcing the same to the village by beating the drum (tattali-kotti) and blowing the trumpet (kālam-lādi)

cells.date: r.y. 5 = c. A.D. 961. January, (Makara, Friday, Punarvasu)
cells.reference: : ARE, 1914, no. 74; SII. XIII, no. 109, p. 53.
cells.match: <button type="button" class="xref-link" data-corpus="sii" data-key="sii|xiii||109" data-url="SII-Inscriptions.html">SII Vol. XIII, No. 109</button>
cells.remarks: Registers gift of 2 plots of land after previous purchase from their original owners to make provision for Chitari, akil, sandal, camphor and neriyasam for fumigation at time of the daily services in the temple of Tirunallur-Mahadeva at Kamaravalli-chaturvedimangalam, a brahmadeya on the north bank. The donor was a Balasiriyan Bhattan Sivan Kuttan of Adanur a devadana-Brahmadeya of Innambar-nadu. The land was declared tax-free by the penunguri-Penumakkal of Kamarasavalli-chaturvedimangalam who met at the temple mandapa after being called by blowing of double-trumpets. The land was irrigated by a channel called Kodandarama-vaykkal and was situated to the east of the channel called Cholamahadevi-vadi. A madhyastha called Arangan Tirumalirunjolai alias Elunurru-aimbattaruvan wrote the document.

cells.reference: ARE, 1920, no. 91; Ibid., Part II, para. 23.
cells.remarks: Records the gift of house - at Tirumalavādi to Kuṇrurudaiyān Terri Periyān alias Edirilichōļamūvendavēļān who owned lands to Kuṇrak-kūṇram alias Uttungatonga-Valanāđu, but who was required to reside in Tirumalavādi guarding the place. He repaired the nritta-maṇdapa in the temple of the Tirumāļa-vāđi-Uđaiyār, the Vishnu temple with its maṇdapa and the Tāyilunallāṇ-maṇdapa by extending their area and improving their general appearance. he replanned the village and opened the street called Vikrama-Chōļaṇ tiruvīdi by filling up a large pit in the centre of the village. He also protected the village from the inundations of the river Kollīdam by removing further south the southern embankment at the spot where the river turning to the north was likely to damage the village during floods. For these meritorious acts of his, he was requested to live in the village of Tirumalavādi and a house was given to him to live in.
